clauses.reason: The operative lead says: "do hereby adopt and approve the report, recommendations and findings of the xldministrator and do order that the said Code of Fair Competition be and it is hereby approved subject to the following conditions". It is a section 3 approval of the Code of Fair Competition for the Graphic Arts Industries, so its operative effect was the code's legal force. Under section 3(b) of the Act the approved code's provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade or industry, under 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations, and under 3(f) a violation was a misdemeanor; that force was the whole operative effect of an approval. The order states no period, condition, 'until' date, stay or provisional approval of its own, and no held record cancels, suspends, modifies under section 10(b) or supersedes the code before June 14, 1935 (see earlier_end_check). Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 (Pub. Res. No. 26, 74th Cong., 49 Stat. 375, approved June 14, 1935) provides: "All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed". The resolution states no effective date other than its approval on June 14, 1935. Repeal of the power to approve codes and of the provisions enforcing them removed the legal force that the approval gave the code, so this clause ended on June 14, 1935; effective date confirmed. The approval is conditional on clauses 1 to 6; those conditions and the President's published statement are treated as separate clauses. June 16, 1935, Title I's original two-year expiry, is not an end date: section 1 of the resolution replaced it with April 1, 1936. A. L. A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, decided May 27, 1935, held the section 3 delegation unconstitutional; it is recorded as a validity characterization (an approval made under an unconstitutional delegation was void from issuance under the doctrine then prevailing), not as an end date, because the decision cancelled no approving order and no held record shows this code cancelled or suspended on May 27, 1935.

clauses.reason: Condition 6 says: "That pending the formulation of a compact or code between the several states of the United States to insure the sale of prison made products on a fair competitive basis with products not so made the provisions of paragraph (g) of Section 26 of the Code applicable to institutions of states or political subdivisions thereof, be and they are hereby stayed for ninety (90) days, or further at the discretion of the Administrator". This is a stay with a stated term of ninety days. The clause states no other start date and, unlike conditions 3 and 5, does not run from the code's effective date, so the ninety days run from the order's date, February 17, 1934: day 90 is May 18, 1934 (February 18 as day 1). The stay therefore ended on its own terms on May 18, 1934, recorded inclusive (the stay runs through that day); counting February 17 itself as day 1 gives May 17, and the exclusive reading (the stay lapsed when May 18 began) is the alternative, so the end falls on May 17, 18 or 19, 1934 under the possible counts and is recorded as May 18 under the owner's inclusive convention. The words 'or further at the discretion of the Administrator' allow a later extension by the Administrator's own act; no held order text or other held record shows one (a search of every held order text for paragraph (g) of Section 26 and for prison-made products finds no later action on it), so under the owner's evidence rule the stated term is the first end and any extension would be a later event. The stay is a command on a code provision, so it could not outlast June 14, 1935 in any case: the S.J. Res. 113 section 2 repeal of June 14, 1935 is a later event for this clause. June 16, 1935, Title I's original two-year expiry, is not an end date: section 1 of the resolution replaced it with April 1, 1936.

EO 6606-B (1934-02-17, Franklin D. Roosevelt), read in full in the held American Presidency Project transcription (registered grade mirror_transcription, not an original; 6218 characters). Identity: the census register lists it as 'Executive Order 6606-B—Code of Fair Competition for the Graphic Arts Industries' dated 1934-02-17; the WPA 1944 list has '1934 Feb 17 p.568: Code of Fair Competition for the Graphic Arts Indus triesconditionallyapproved. VII NRA Codes 1.'. Page check: the mirror page record with the same source sha256 is headed 'Executive Order 6606-B—Code of Fair Competition for the Graphic Arts Industries', dated 1934-02-17, from a common-crawl capture of 2026-01-23T05:14:01Z, and its text_sha256 equals the held text's; the heading names this order's number and the date and subject agree with the text. Machine inventory corrected (see each clause's inventory_reason): the machine clause 1 contains two commands (the deletion of section 24 with transfer of powers, and a proviso authorizing a Labor Board), and machine clause 6 runs on through the signature block into the President's published statement, which is its own command. Nine clauses result: the approval, conditions 1 (two parts), 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and the published statement. Operative lead: the President orders "that the said Code of Fair Competition be and it is hereby approved subject to the following conditions": the Code of Fair Competition for the Graphic Arts Industries (title I, section 3(a)). Eight clauses depend on the approved code and end with it on June 14, 1935 (S.J. Res. 113 section 2). Condition 6 is a stay of paragraph (g) of Section 26 of the code "for ninety (90) days, or further at the discretion of the Administrator", which has its own fixed term and ends earlier, on May 18, 1934 by its own terms; no held record shows an extension.

savings.reason: Acts done under the approved code before June 14, 1935, and any liability for violating it before that date, are accrued effects. The general savings statute of the time (not a held source) preserved liabilities already incurred under a repealed statute; that preservation does not keep the approval operative. Section 5 of the Act exempted from the antitrust laws "any code, agreement, or license approved, prescribed, or issued and in effect under this title" and complying action while Title I was in effect and for sixty days after; whatever exemption survives for action taken before the repeal is an accrued effect. The proviso in section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 says the exemption "shall extend only to agreements and action thereunder" of two kinds (section 7(a) requirements, and prohibiting practices already unlawful); it names agreements, not codes, and states no time limit, so the held text does not settle whether it narrowed the exemption for action taken under codes before June 14, 1935. No held source continues this approval after June 14, 1935 and no held source shows a prosecution continued after that date.
